ai.title: Branchial Cyst
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A branchial cyst is a congenital neck mass arising from remnants of the branchial apparatus. It presents as a painless, fluctuant swelling, often in the lateral neck, and requires careful evaluation to exclude infection or malignancy.

b: Usually present in late childhood to early adulthood
Typically a solitary, soft, non‑tender mass
May become infected after upper respiratory infection
sections.p: Branchial cysts are developmental anomalies that result from incomplete involution of the branchial (pharyngeal) clefts during embryogenesis. They are most common in the second branchial cleft, appearing along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

b: Location: along the anterior border of SCM, near the angle of the mandible
Differential: cystic hygroma, thyroglossal duct cyst, infected lymph node, metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on clinical pattern, imaging, and exclusion of other cystic neck lesions. In low‑resource settings, ultrasound is the primary tool; CT or MRI are reserved for atypical cases.

b: Infection can mimic a bacterial neck abscess
Rare malignant transformation (e.g., carcinoma arising in a cyst) warrants histology
sections.p: While benign, branchial cysts can cause cosmetic concern, airway compression if large, or secondary infection. Prompt recognition avoids unnecessary antibiotics and guides definitive surgical excision.

t.b: Is the lesion cystic and where is it located? → Confirms cystic nature, assesses size, septations, and relation to vessels.
What is the fluid composition? → Straw‑coloured fluid supports cyst; presence of pus suggests infection; atypical cells raise suspicion of malignancy.
Is there deep extension or involvement of vital structures? → Defines anatomy for surgical planning.
Has the cyst been completely removed and is there any malignant change? → Confirms diagnosis and rules out carcinoma.

b: Antibiotics: cover common skin flora and anaerobes; avoid macrolides alone due to limited anaerobic coverage
Surgical excision: careful dissection of the tract, often via a transverse cervical incision
Post‑operative care: monitor for wound infection, ensure drainage if needed
sections.p: First treat infection with appropriate antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) and drainage if abscessed. Definitive therapy is complete surgical excision of the cyst and tract to prevent recurrence.

b: Key history: gradual swelling, recent URI, any pain or discharge
Physical exam: mobile, non‑pulsatile, fluctuant mass lateral to SCM
When imaging unavailable: rely on clinical location and FNA characteristics
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, differential diagnosis, and steps when imaging is limited.

b: Assuming all neck cysts are infectious and prescribing antibiotics alone
Incomplete excision of the tract → high recurrence rate
Failing to send excised tissue for histology
sections.p: Misidentifying a branchial cyst as a simple lymph node or a thyroid nodule can lead to inappropriate treatment.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid increase in size with airway compromise
High fever, neck swelling with signs of sepsis
Neurological deficits (e.g., hoarseness, dysphagia) suggesting deep structure involvement
